passage:
Yusuf had forty rupees in his tin, and the shop window held a remote-control car that cost four hundred. Every Sunday he stood in front of it. His friends bought sweets and sticker packets. Yusuf's fingers twitched near a pack of cricket cards.
"Buy it, beta, it's your money," said his mother Binita.
"I'll wait," said Yusuf.
"Next month?"
"Maybe two."
At home he drew ten squares on a sheet of paper and coloured one in each time he added coins. Binita had told him the shopkeeper would keep the car aside for him, and every Sunday the shopkeeper nodded at the window.
Three months later Yusuf carried the box home, and it felt heavier and better than any sweet.

qa.q: How many rupees did Yusuf have in his tin at the start?
qa.a: Forty rupees.

qa.q: What is Yusuf feeling as he stands at the shop window and passes the cricket cards?
qa.a: He is tempted but determined. His fingers twitch near the cards, yet he says he will wait for the car.

qa.q: What choice helped Yusuf keep saving?
qa.a: He drew ten squares and coloured one each time he added coins, so his progress was visible, and he trusted that the shopkeeper would keep the car aside.

qa.q: How might Binita feel watching Yusuf choose to wait?
qa.a: Probably proud and a little amazed, since she says it is his money but he decides to wait.

grounding: A child saves pocket money for a bigger toy instead of spending it, trusting the reward will arrive.

passage:
Vaibhav: Tarun, look, the fair has jalebis! Aren't you buying one?
Tarun: No, Mama. I'm saving for the football.
Vaibhav: One jalebi won't hurt.
Tarun: Last time you said, "Wait till Diwali," and you did take me. So I believe you'll take me for the football too.
Vaibhav: I will. How much have you got?
Tarun: Eighty-five rupees. Two more months.
Vaibhav: That's a long time.
Tarun: It's okay. I look at the picture every night. And I keep the coins in a tin, so I can't cheat.
Vaibhav: Then I'll buy the jalebi and you hold it while I eat.
Tarun: Ha! Deal.

qa.q: How many rupees does Tarun have saved?
qa.a: Eighty-five rupees.

qa.q: Why is Tarun able to say no to the jalebi, and what is Tarun feeling about the football?
qa.a: Tarun feels confident and hopeful because Vaibhav kept the earlier promise about Diwali, so Tarun trusts the football promise too.

qa.q: What habits help Tarun keep waiting?
qa.a: Tarun looks at the football picture every night and keeps the coins in a tin so they cannot be spent.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav be thinking when Tarun mentions the Diwali promise?
qa.a: Vaibhav may feel touched and a little responsible, since Tarun's patience depends on Vaibhav keeping the promise.

grounding: A child chooses to save for a bigger reward, trusting that promised rewards actually arrive.

passage:
Every Saturday in Lisbon, Rafael got a few coins for helping at his aunt Clara's café, and every Saturday he walked past the sweet shop on the way home. For three weeks he spent it all on gummy sweets.
Then he saw a real leather football in the sports shop window. Clara helped him draw a chart on the café's back wall: ten squares, one for each Saturday. "Put the coins in this jar. I'll keep it on the shelf. It'll be here, I promise."
The first two Saturdays were hard. He stood outside the sweet shop for a long time. But each week the jar was exactly where Clara said, and heavier.
On the tenth Saturday they walked to the sports shop together. Rafael carried the football all the way home as if it were made of glass.

qa.q: How many squares were on the chart?
qa.a: Ten squares, one for each Saturday.

qa.q: What was Rafael feeling outside the sweet shop on the first Saturdays?
qa.a: Rafael felt tempted and torn, standing there a long time before walking on.

qa.q: What helped Rafael keep saving?
qa.a: The chart made progress visible, and Clara kept the jar safe each week exactly as promised, so he could trust the reward would come.

qa.q: How might Clara feel walking to the sports shop with him?
qa.a: Clara probably felt proud and happy to see her nephew's patience pay off.

grounding: Shows a child choosing to save for a bigger toy instead of spending, helped by trust that the promise will hold.

passage:
Every Monday at Mahima's school, the savings club met in the library. Children dropped coins into their own labelled tins, and Mrs Rao wrote each total in a little book. Mahima was saving for a science kit with a real magnifying glass.
Jatin, from her class, jingled his coins outside the canteen. "Samosa? Come on, you can save next week."
Mahima's stomach rumbled. She looked at the samosas, then at her tin. Last term her tin had grown just as Mrs Rao's book said it would; not one coin had gone missing.
"In four weeks I'll have enough," she said, and dropped the coins in.
Four Mondays later, Mrs Rao handed her the tin, and Mahima and her mother bought the kit that evening.

qa.q: What was Mahima saving for?
qa.a: A science kit with a real magnifying glass.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when Jatin offered a samosa?
qa.a: Mahima felt tempted, stomach rumbling, but trusted her savings would grow as they had before.

qa.q: What helped Mahima choose later over now?
qa.a: Seeing last term that her tin grew exactly as Mrs Rao's book said, so she trusted the reward would come.

qa.q: How might Jatin see Mahima's choice?
qa.a: Jatin seems to think she's missing out, tempting her to put saving off till next week.

grounding: Shows a child choosing to save for something bigger instead of spending now, backed by trust that savings are kept safe.

passage:
June. Ishita, nine, wanted a bicycle. Uma Paati said, "Save your festival money, and I'll add the same amount at Diwali." Ishita wasn't sure. Last year Mama had promised a doll and forgotten.
August. At Raksha Bandhan, Ishita got money from three uncles. The ice-cream man rang his bell outside. She stood at the gate, then went in and put the notes in Paati's steel box. Paati chalked the amount on the lid.
November. After Diwali, Paati opened the box, counted, and added exactly the same amount from her own purse, as promised. Ishita rode the new red bicycle round the colony three times, ringing the bell.

qa.q: Where did Ishita put her Raksha Bandhan money?
qa.a: In Paati's steel box.

qa.q: Why was Ishita unsure in June?
qa.a: She was doubtful, because last year Mama had promised a doll and forgotten.

qa.q: What helped Ishita's patience grow?
qa.a: Paati chalked the amount on the lid each time and kept her word at Diwali, so Ishita could trust the reward.

qa.q: How might Uma Paati feel watching Ishita ride the bicycle?
qa.a: Uma Paati likely feels happy and proud that her promise and Ishita's waiting both came through.

grounding: Shows a child choosing to save for a bigger thing over months, with patience growing from trust that a promise will be kept.

passage: Tarun, you count your coins every evening, so let me tell you something. When I was about your age, your Dada gave me two rupees every Sunday. In Hari's shop window there was a wooden cricket bat with a proper rubber grip. Every Sunday the sweet cart rang its bell outside our gate, and every Sunday my hands itched. I kept the coins in an old tea tin under my bed. Twice I opened it for jalebis and felt cheated afterwards. But Dada had said he would add a little once I reached halfway, and he did, the very week I got there. That was when I believed the bat was really coming. Eleven weeks later, your Tushar Chacha walked into that shop and paid for it himself.

qa.q: Where did Tushar keep the coins he was saving?
qa.a: He kept them in an old tea tin under his bed.

qa.q: What was young Tushar feeling each Sunday when the sweet cart rang its bell?
qa.a: He felt tempted and restless, because his hands itched to spend the coins, and when he did buy jalebis he felt cheated afterwards.

qa.q: Which moment in the story helped Tushar keep saving, and why?
qa.a: When Dada added the money at the halfway point as he had said, Tushar saw the promise was real, so waiting began to feel worth it.

qa.q: How might Dada have felt when he kept his word that week?
qa.a: He was probably pleased to see the boy stick with his plan, and knew that keeping his word would help him trust the next promise too.

grounding: Illustrates a child choosing to save for a bigger toy instead of spending, helped by trust that a promised reward really came.
